page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 5 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Author Purpose, Rhetoric, and Craft Choices

Lesson Focus

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.RHT.01 — align purpose, audience, rhetorical strategy, and craft choices in creative work.

What You Will Learn

  • Distinguish topic, purpose, message, and intended effect.
  • Analyze how credibility, reasoning, emotion, and timing operate in creative texts.
  • Select craft choices that fit a specific audience and situation.
  • Revise manipulative, mismatched, or ethically weak persuasion.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 5 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.

TermMeaningExample
author purposeThe result a writer intends to produce for a particular audience.The author’s purpose is to persuade readers to support the library.
audienceThe specific readers or listeners a work addresses or anticipates.A writer adjusts examples for an audience of younger students.
rhetoricThe purposeful use of language, form, evidence, and arrangement to influence understanding or response.The speech uses rhetoric to shape how listeners understand the proposal.
ethosAn appeal based on credibility, character, or trustworthiness.Citing experience as a firefighter builds ethos.
logosAn appeal based on reasons, evidence, patterns, or causal logic.Statistics about response times appeal to logos.
pathosAn appeal to emotion, values, or imagination.A story about a displaced family appeals to pathos.
kairosThe strategic use of timing, urgency, and situation.Delivering the argument before the vote takes advantage of kairos.
rhetorical situationThe relationship among writer, audience, purpose, context, and constraints.The speaker, audience, purpose, and occasion form the rhetorical situation.
intended effectThe response or understanding a writer aims to create.The intended effect is for readers to question the policy.
craft choiceA deliberate decision about structure, viewpoint, diction, syntax, imagery, detail, or pacing.Repeating one sentence at key moments is a deliberate craft choice.
manipulationInfluence that distorts evidence, exploits vulnerability, or blocks informed judgment.Hiding important evidence to provoke fear becomes manipulation.
rhetorical alignmentA clear fit among purpose, audience, evidence, form, and style.Formal language and verified data create rhetorical alignment with a skeptical audience.

Vocabulary Application — Try It

Use each sentence’s context to place the correct term. Choose Check, study the result, and retry any missed item. This is ungraded practice.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 5 | Page 3 of 6

Direct Teaching: Aligning Purpose, Audience, and Craft

Seven-Step Rhetorical Craft Method

  1. Name the audience precisely.
  2. State the purpose as an action: reassure, challenge, expose, invite, or persuade.
  3. Define the intended effect.
  4. Identify the situation, constraints, and timing.
  5. Select ethical appeals and evidence.
  6. Choose craft elements that carry those appeals.
  7. Audit alignment and unintended effects.

Visual Rhetorical Alignment Map

AUDIENCEPURPOSEAPPEAL + EVIDENCECRAFT CHOICEEFFECT
Who → Why now → What support → How presented → What response
Learning routes: color-code the five stages; rehearse the chain aloud; or arrange strategy cards beneath the audience and purpose.

Pause and Choose: Align Appeal with Audience

A student asks the library board to test later evening hours. Which opening coordinates ethos, logos, and pathos for that audience?

A. “Adults clearly do not care whether teenagers have a safe place to study.”
Not the best choice. The accusation stereotypes the audience, offers no evidence, and makes cooperation less likely. Emotional force does not substitute for a defensible appeal.
B. “At closing, twelve students moved unfinished work to the unlit bus stop. Usage logs show this pattern on most weekdays; we request a thirty-day trial that accounts for staffing limits.”
✓ Correct—the appeals reinforce one purpose. The scene clarifies human stakes, the data supports reasoning, and the fair acknowledgment plus limited request builds credibility with the board.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Appeal-to-Craft Table

AppealCreative evidenceEthical check
Ethosspecific experience, fair acknowledgmentIs credibility earned?
Logoscausal chain, comparison, concrete patternIs reasoning complete?
Pathosscene, image, human stakesDoes emotion illuminate evidence?
Kairosdeadline, occasion, urgent turnIs urgency genuine?

Purpose Is Not Topic

Topic: school lunch. Weak purpose: “to talk about lunch.” Precise purpose: “to help families see how a shortened lunch period affects students with mobility needs and support a schedule revision.”

Ethical Persuasion

  • Represent opposing evidence fairly.
  • Do not fabricate urgency or certainty.
  • Let emotional detail clarify stakes rather than replace reasoning.
  • Anticipate audiences without stereotyping them.
  • Give readers enough context for informed judgment.

Pause and Choose: Use Urgency Ethically

The board meets next month, but no immediate closure is planned. Which sentence uses kairos without fabricating a crisis?

A. “Unless you approve this tonight, students will permanently lose their chance to succeed.”
Not the best choice. It invents a deadline and an absolute consequence. False urgency weakens credibility and prevents informed judgment.
B. “A trial approved at next month’s meeting could begin before winter’s shorter daylight hours increase the need for a safe evening study space.”
✓ Correct—the timing is genuine and relevant. The sentence connects the actual decision window to a foreseeable condition without exaggerating certainty or forcing agreement.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Common Failures

  • Choosing techniques before defining purpose.
  • Calling any sad detail pathos without explaining its function.
  • Treating ethos, logos, and pathos as separate boxes rather than interacting appeals.
  • Using a generalized “everyone” audience.
  • Confusing persuasion with guaranteed agreement.

Pause and Try — Build an Ethical Appeal

Situation: A student wants the library board to extend evening hours. The draft begins by accusing adults of not caring about teenagers.

Your turn: Name the audience and purpose. Then replace the accusation with one ethical appeal that uses a purposeful craft choice.

Check your thinking with the teacher model

The audience is the library board; the purpose is to win approval for a trial extension. I would open with a brief scene of students leaving at closing time, add reliable usage data, acknowledge staffing limits, and request a thirty-day pilot.

Why this works: The scene creates measured pathos, the data supplies logos, and the fair acknowledgment builds ethos. The form and tone respect the audience instead of manipulating it.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 5 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Rhetorical Craft Decisions

Example 1 — Personal Scene With Evidence

A student writes to the transit board about a missing late bus.

  1. Audience: board members controlling routes.
  2. Purpose: support a three-month pilot.
  3. Pathos: one scene shows a custodian waiting after midnight.
  4. Logos: missed-shift data reveals a pattern.
  5. Ethos: the writer acknowledges cost constraints.
  6. Kairos: budget hearing occurs Friday.
  7. Craft: scene opens attention; concise comparison moves toward action.

Example 2 — Revise Manipulative Emotion

Weak: “Only a heartless person could close the garden where children dream.”

  1. Problem: attacks audience character and substitutes emotion for evidence.
  2. Revision: describe one class measuring soil recovery.
  3. Add evidence: participation and maintenance costs.
  4. Acknowledge the competing need for parking.
  5. Purposeful pathos: show what use looks like.
  6. Ethical effect: invite judgment rather than shame disagreement.

Example 3 — Same Evidence, Different Audience

A story about water restrictions addresses residents and engineers.

  1. Residents need recognizable household stakes and clear choices.
  2. Engineers need measurement, uncertainty, and system constraints.
  3. Both versions preserve the same facts.
  4. Resident craft: close focalized scene and plain diction.
  5. Engineer craft: causal structure and precise quantities.
  6. Alignment changes form, not truth.

Model Grid

ModelPrimary revisionGain
Transitcoordinate appealsactionable case
Gardenreplace attack with evidenceethical credibility
Wateradapt form to audiencerelevance without distortion

Choose A or B — Which Appeal Is Better Aligned?

Purpose: Persuade the library board to test later evening hours.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which appeal is better aligned to a library board considering later evening hours?

A. The board clearly does not care about students, and everyone will suffer unless it keeps the library open late immediately.
Weaker response. This accusation relies on exaggerated emotion, weakens the writer’s credibility, and ignores the board’s practical concerns.
B. A four-week evening-hours pilot would serve students whose work schedules limit daytime access; attendance counts and staffing costs could then guide a permanent decision.
Stronger response. This proposal combines audience-aware evidence, a reasonable action, measurable results, and respectful tone, strengthening logos and ethos while acknowledging student needs.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Your Turn — Identify the appeals, then check

The human scene is pathos; verified counts are logos; acknowledging constraints builds ethos; proposing a limited pilot now uses kairos. Together they create rhetorical alignment rather than manipulation.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 5 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Author Purpose, Rhetoric, and Craft Choices

Purpose

Shape language and craft choices deliberately for a specific audience and purpose.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Your work should show deliberate choices, not just completion.

Source for Your Work

A town council plans to close the only public garden. A teenager speaks at the meeting because the garden is both a community gathering place and the last green space near an elementary school.

1. Plan Before You Draft

DecisionYour Plan
Character goal and obstacleWrite one clear sentence.
Key turning pointState the choice or discovery.
Meaning readers should inferName the idea without writing a moral.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach would produce stronger creative writing? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. The garden is nice and everyone likes it, so the council should keep it open.
B. On summer afternoons, children measure tomato vines where traffic once drowned out conversation; closing the garden would erase both a classroom and a meeting place.

3. Apply the Lesson

Write a 250–350 word persuasive monologue for the teenager. Establish a clear purpose, address the council as the audience, and use two rhetorical appeals plus intentional diction and imagery.

4. Revise with Purpose

Revise one weak appeal. Name whether you strengthened credibility, emotion, or logic and explain how the new wording better serves the purpose.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your creative work applies the lesson skill and uses the source provided.
  • Your explanation names a specific choice and its effect.
  • Your revision improves meaning or craft, not only spelling.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Author Purpose, Rhetoric, and Craft Choices

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original writing, and explain your craft decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Last Archive

“If we sell the archive,” Devon told the council, “we do not simply lose shelves of paper. We lose the letters that prove who built this town, the flood records that can protect our homes, and the voices our children have not heard yet. I have spent six months cataloging those records with trained historians. Give us one year to turn this room into a public resource before you turn it into storage.”

Author purpose is the effect a writer intends to create. Ethos builds credibility, pathos appeals to emotion, and logos uses reasons and evidence.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Identify Devon’s audience and purpose. Then cite one example of ethos, pathos, or logos and explain how it serves that purpose.
  2. How do the concrete details about letters, flood records, and children strengthen the appeal more than a general claim would?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which statement is better tailored to persuade the council, and why?

A. The archive matters a lot, and everyone should agree with me.
B. The flood records can protect homes, and the letters preserve voices future residents deserve to hear.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Write a 400–500 word persuasive monologue spoken by a character facing an important decision.

  1. Opening: Establish the audience, situation, and a clear claim.
  2. Body: Develop the claim with at least two rhetorical appeals and specific evidence.
  3. Counterpoint: Acknowledge one reasonable objection and respond to it.
  4. Conclusion: Synthesize the strongest reason and end with a purposeful call or final image.

Label two sentences to show which rhetorical appeals they use and explain why each fits the audience.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the reader should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Revise one appeal that is too general. Add a precise detail, reason, or image that better fits the audience and purpose.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise the organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the writing becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The writing follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
